justification: A dies on “at least ninety-two per cent of its sailings berth within ten minutes of the booked minute” — neither “every” nor “exactly” survives that span. B dies on the dates: the payment has run “Since 2011” while the relief boat’s certificate ran out “in 2016”. D is the strong trap because penalising cancellation is what a reader expects of the world, and the text explicitly inverts it: “A sailing that does not run is not late; it leaves the count altogether”, with Q1 2023 losing forty-one sailings and posting “ninety-seven per cent, the highest it had ever been” — cancellations raise the figure, so nothing is reduced.

B dies on “The median crossing that year took twenty-four minutes against an eighteen-minute booking” — a median licenses no claim about every sailing, and the published seventy-one per cent shows the fleet was not uniformly outside the band. C dies on the same span plus “a promise nobody could keep” and “five of the nine added minutes only brought the book level with the boat”; no weather qualification attaches to 2005 anywhere in the text. D dies on “The published reliability figure stood at seventy-one per cent in 2005” — lateness was being measured and published at the time. Set shape gives nothing away: C hedges (“broadly”, “except”) at least as much as key A.

A dies on “the relief boat’s passenger certificate ran out and the company did not replace her” — declining to replace is not selling, and no disposal appears anywhere. B dies on the same span, which supplies a passive cause (an expiring certificate) and no intention; lengthening headways is a cost the operator complains of, not an aim. C dies twice, on Cottam’s own hedge “nearly the whole of it” and on the writer’s “the interval between departures went from twenty-five minutes to thirty-two … Some of the frequency was gone before the boat was”. Key D is carried by arithmetic spanning two paragraphs: padding moved the interval 25→32, the lost boat moved it 32→70.

A dies on “Cottam’s account has a soft place in the same decade” together with the untimed ninety seconds — the writer does not settle it for the operator. C dies on “an explanation that fits without having been tested” and “Until somebody can”, which concede the fit and leave the test open, and on “Nobody disputes the stamps”. D is the best challenger — the piece is largely three sources given their say — but dies because the final paragraph is unattributed writer’s voice delivering judgements (“Where Cattermay’s case thins is the join”, “Cottam’s account has a soft place”); being even-handed between two sources is not withholding judgement. Key B is carried by “Nobody disputes the stamps … does not contest the fifteen minutes” set against “the timetable is an explanation that fits without having been tested”.

A is a true detail (2013 linkspan rebuild, the ninety-second locking sequence) confined to two sentences, while the passage’s frame is the 71→96 reliability figure — a true-but-narrow option, which is the legitimate shape of a main-idea distractor. B dies on scope: only the Brackenhithe crossing is ever discussed, no other service and no national trend. C is the nearest miss and dies on “Nobody disputes the stamps” and “Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing, and does not contest the fifteen minutes” — the ticket data yields a firm, agreed conclusion; what resists conclusion is the causal join, not the data. C also drops the reliability figure and Bexwarden’s cancelled-sailings strand entirely, both of which key D carries.

“do a brisk trade” is the fixed collocation, and the context measures volume, not speed (“three hundred and forty of them go out”, “from eleven until the light goes”). A dies because “hasty” means done in a hurry and carelessly and does not collocate with “trade”. B dies because “rapid” measures rate of motion or change, not a day’s takings. C dies because “swift” describes a single quick action, not sustained business. No free elimination is available: all four options mean “quick”, so the discriminator is the collocation itself, i.e. the knowledge under test.

The frame is a perfect of intransitive “lie” — “had ___ there since breakfast” — so only the past participle “lain” fits. A dies because a bare infinitive cannot follow “had”. D dies for the same reason: “lay” is the simple past of “lie”, not its participle. C is the familiar usage trap, but “laid” is the participle of transitive “lay” and demands an object the clause does not have. Pure grammar gap, no textual ambiguity.

The preceding sentence, “The hire is the whole of the transaction”, already states the nominal position, so the gap must introduce the observed counterpart — and what follows is an observed fact (“the one staffed thing on the mile”, “the one person on it who is stationary and paid”), with the nominal-versus-actual frame set up earlier by “What the pitch charges for and what it does are not the same thing”. A is the only real challenger and dies because it would make the second clause the principle rather than the practice, and being the one staffed thing on a mile of beach is a fact, not a principle. B dies because nothing is given in exchange for the ten-pence rise. D dies because there is no prior action for anything to precede.

findings: D: “confesses” is a live alternative — “Pressed on whether she minds the questions” sets up exactly the reluctant admission “confess” denotes, and admitting the questions are an obstruction is mildly discreditable for someone paid to be approachable; it is killed only by the coordinated second conjunct and by connotation, which is a subtle reading.
justification: A is right and D is arguable. The case FOR D at full strength: “Pressed on” establishes that she is being pushed, so the verb must denote a reluctant admission, and “confesses” denotes that as squarely as “concedes”; the content admitted — that the questions are an obstruction — is a mildly discreditable attitude for someone whose pitch depends on being approachable, which is confess’s natural territory. What kills D is narrower than the item deserves. The verb governs a coordinated object, “that in August they are an obstruction and by late September most of the job”, and the second conjunct is an analytical reframing of her own work, not a fault: nobody confesses that questions are most of the job. “Concedes” also carries the yielding-a-point-to-an-interlocutor sense that “Pressed on” asks for, and the closing “Gregson would not put it that way” confirms she is in a mildly argumentative posture with the writer. So the key is better, but a candidate choosing “confesses” relies on a real sense of the word and is beaten only on connotation plus the coordination test — survivable with effort. B and C do die cleanly: “boasts” is contradicted by the unflattering content and by “Pressed on”, and “volunteers” means unprompted, the exact antonym of “Pressed on”.

findings: A/B/C: “widely”, “routinely” and “heavily” are mutually substitutable in this frame, so none can be uniquely correct and the key is reachable by elimination without reading the passage. The leak is in the set shape, not in any distractor’s defensibility.
justification: On the text all three distractors die cleanly and identically: the concessive “but”, plus “and it shut after its second summer”, plus the later explanation that “A counter has to be approached, and approaching one is a decision you have to justify”, all require a negative degree adverb, and “widely”, “routinely” and “heavily” are all positive. That identical death is the problem. The three are interchangeable here, so a test-wise candidate reasons that no one of them can be the unique key and takes the sole option of opposite polarity — “barely” — without consulting the passage. Contrast gap (1), where all four options mean “quick” and eliminating three requires knowing the “brisk trade” collocation, i.e. the very knowledge under test; here eliminating three requires none. The key is correct and the passage supports it unambiguously; the flag is that the option set alone gives it away. This is the same species as the “key is the only hedged option” failure the batch was authored against, transposed into a cloze gap.

findings: B: “The plaice left the bag as readily as the haddock once the meshes were turned” is survivable — the passage’s own explanation, “a flat fish and a stretched mesh being much the same shape”, entails that the plaice were already passing the diamond meshes, so after the turn both species are leaving the bag. B is killed by the contrastive framing and by the unstated rate comparison, not by any statement that plaice were retained.
justification: Mechanism check first, since a backwards mechanism would make key D wrong: the passage is correct, not backwards. Diamond meshes do elongate along the tow axis under drag and close laterally (“every mesh pulls long and thin … is a slot by then”), which is exactly why raising mesh size in a diamond cod end buys far less roundfish escape than the size measured on deck predicts; re-hanging the netting so the meshes stand as squares under load — “the same twine turned right round the bag”, i.e. turned-mesh / T90 — is the standard real remedy, and it works for round-bodied gadoids like haddock precisely because a round fish “has to get its width through”, while leaving flatfish roughly where they were because a flat body already matches an elongated slot. The closing loss of marketable fish “on the tows when the square bars ran slack” is also true to the gear. Key D therefore stands. A dies flat on “waited for the small haddock to see themselves out. They did not” and “the boxes at the harbour looked much as they had the year before”. C dies on “He had the same twine turned right round the bag” — the whole bag was re-hung, no panel was inserted and no netting was added; C names the commoner real-world solution (a square-mesh panel in the top of the cod end) and is wrong only per the text, which is fair because the text is explicit about what he did. B is the flag. FOR B at full strength: the text never says plaice were being retained, and its stated reason for “The plaice were much as before” — that a flat fish and a stretched mesh are much the same shape — entails they were already getting through the diamond meshes; after the turn the small haddock go out too, so on this reading both are leaving and B is descriptively true of the post-turn bag. AGAINST: the two sentences are set in explicit contrast (“The small haddock went out. The plaice were much as before.”), so the plain reading is that the turn changed everything for the haddock and nothing for the plaice — which is what B denies by tying the plaice’s escape to “once the meshes were turned”; and the passage offers no rate comparison licensing “as readily as”. B is wrong, but a candidate who works the shape logic through can defend it. The item would be safe if B asserted plaice retention outright rather than an unstated equivalence.

Key A is carried by arithmetic the text supplies in full: no term ran for anything but seven years, each second binding “ran its seven years from the day of sealing” and “fell three to six years after the first”, so in all five cases the second term ends three to six years past the first term’s expiry — Ward’s 1751+7 = 1758 against 1755+7 = 1762 — and “The second entries were not continuations” blocks the escape that the first term had simply run out. B dies flat on “Each of the first masters went on enrolling boys of his own for years afterwards”: no first master gave up his trade. C dies on the enumeration of the five fathers — “two lived in the town, one farmed nine miles off, one combed wool in the next county, and one the clerk left unplaced” — so at most two of five. D dies on “In three of the five the second premium was the larger sum”, and is contradicted in the worked example too (eleven pounds then fourteen). All four options are stated flat, so no hedging asymmetry marks the key.

Key C is the rule as stated: “rännan skulle luta mindre än marken nedanför den”, confirmed by the measurement “drygt en halv meter på fyrahundra, medan myrytan under den faller ungefär det dubbla”. A dies on the closing contrast “en vattningsränna går tvärs över sluttningen och faller nästan inte alls, ett dike går rakt nedför den” — straight downslope is the drainage ditch, the thing the watering channel is defined against. B dies on the same rule sentence, “luta mindre än marken”. D dies on “Hela konsten låg i avvägningen” and on the consequence clause “Först då lämnade vattnet rännan längs hela dess längd i stället för att följa den till den lägsta punkten och skära sig ner där” — free placement is precisely the failure the rule exists to prevent.

Key B restates the causal chain the text marks as decisive: “Det avgörande var syret. Rinnande vatten tillför hela tiden syre … nedbrytningen av torven går fortare, och den näring som frigörs ur myren själv blir tillgänglig för växterna.” A is the inversion and dies on “Stillastående vatten gör tvärtom: det stänger ute luften, nedbrytningen avstannar och marken surnar” — preserved peat is the failure case, not the mechanism. C reverses the arrow (nutrients oxygenating the water rather than oxygen releasing nutrients) and dies on the same chain, which runs strictly syre → nedbrytning → näring. D dies on “Bäckvatten från myrmark är brunt och slamfattigt. Någon nämnvärd mängd mineraljord avlagrades inte på ängarna vid Vråbäcken”, and again on “utan gödsel gick åkern tillbaka”. Silt irrigation is a genuine mechanism and the text concedes it works elsewhere (“Längs de grumligare åarna i söder vägde slammet tyngre än här”), which is what makes D a fair trap rather than a live answer.

The agreement is introduced under “Till detta kom samordningen” and characterised as having “fördelade vattnet i turer om fyra dygn och angav i vilken ordning turerna skulle tas” — key D exactly. A dies because the 1870 suit is reported without any ruling (“stämde två av gårdarna den översta inför häradsrätten” and nothing further), so there is no dom to exemplify, and the 1858 agreement predates the suit by twelve years. B dies on the same span: what was divided in four-day turns was the water, not the hay, and no uneven hay distribution appears anywhere. C dies because the nine hundred dagsverken belong to a different sentence (“Att gräva anläggningen uppges ha tagit omkring niohundra dagsverken fördelade på tre somrar”) and the agreement says nothing about labour — same-paragraph proximity is the whole of C’s appeal.

Key A is carried by the two rebuttals, both of which are source-critical: “Pärlhage invänder att kartorna sällan går att tidfästa närmare än ett par decennier” and “Nolvide invänder att hennes socknar är valda bland dem som har bevarade dikningshandlingar”. B dies on “När och varför bruket upphörde är omtvistat” and on Pärlhage’s dating objection, which is precisely a refusal to let the maps settle it; the premise clause about the maps is true per the text, but “avgjord” is not. C dies because they work from different materials and different samples — “ett fyrtiotal socknar” resting on dikningshandlingar against “karterat rännsystemen i fyra socknar”. D is the sneakiest, since “De två förloppen infaller i de flesta socknar inom samma tjugoårsperiod” does look like convergence, but that coincidence is what prevents the evidence from separating the two causes (“ingen förde bok över hur många dagar som gick åt till rännorna”) — it makes the dispute unresolvable, not unimportant, and the explanations point at different causes (foderekonomi against arbetskraft). Hedging is balanced two-two (A “i första hand” and C “sannolikt” against absolute B and D), so the set shape gives nothing away.

Key C is the calculation the text openly invites with “Räkna gärna själv”: at two kronor per metre, 5,4 km against 1,8 km is exactly three times the bidrag. A dies flat on “det betalades ut till samfälligheten oavsett hur många som bodde vid vägen” and on “Ett bidrag som mäts i meter och inte i hushåll”. B dies on the same figures worked per household — 10 800 kronor across four households against 3 600 across twenty-four, eighteen to one rather than roughly equal — and on “gynnar den som bor glest”. D dies on “betalades ut till samfälligheten”; an entreprenör is indeed paid, but under an arrangement the text separates explicitly (“Den plogningen har för övrigt aldrig legat i bidraget utan i kommunens avtal med entreprenören”), which is what makes D a well-built trap rather than a live answer.

Key B is the article’s whole argument: “Kommunen har alltså haft rätt i sak”, “Jag har inget att invända mot besparingen”, and “Det jag begär är 1,9 kilometer. Låt plogbilen gå ända fram till vändplanen och lägg sträckan i driftbudgeten.” A dies on “Jag tror ändå att den linjen förlorar, och jag tycker inte att den är riktig” — the svek framing is Sarvhed’s, and “Jag förstår henne” concedes sympathy, not agreement; that understanding-is-not-endorsement move is the item’s real discrimination. C dies on “jag begär det inte tillbaka – inte heller ett nytt räknat per hushåll”, which forecloses both restoration and redesign. D dies on the costing, which is deployed against building a vändplan at all (“drygt tio vintrars plogning av just den sträcka kommunen vill sluta ploga”), on the ask being that the kommun keep ploughing instead, and on the land not even being acquired (“Marken är inte inlöst”).

Key B is stated: “Nio plåtar har moln, och även på de korten ligger samma jämna blå himmel över taken”. A dies on that same sentence — “även” is the direct negation of “bara där plåten var tom”, since the nine cloud plates got the identical blue. C dies on “samma jämna blå himmel”, which asserts uniformity, and again on “Vidbring tryckte nya upplagor från samma plåt … och samma anvisning följde med varje gång” — identical views got identical colour. D dies on the plate/card slip it is built from: “På de flesta plåtarna är den en tom vit yta” is true of the plates and false of the cards, and “Himlen ändras på varje kort” sits inside an established plate-against-card frame (“Jag har lagt plåt och kort bredvid varandra”), so it reads as “is altered on every card”, with the next two sentences saying what it was altered to.

Key D is carried across two paragraphs: the August 1919 postmark on a card showing a magasin demolished in autumn 1911, resolved by “Vidbring tryckte nya upplagor från samma plåt så länge ett motiv gick att sälja”. A dies by absence — the firm shot its own glass plates (“Fotograferingen skedde med glasplåt”, forty-one surviving) and no purchase of outside images appears anywhere; buying in stock images is a real publishing practice, so A is right in the world and unsupported by the text, which is fair since the text is explicit about the firm’s own plates. B dies on “samma anvisning följde med varje gång” — the motif was reused unchanged, not remade per edition. C is the nearest miss, since long shelf life would genuinely explain a late postmark, but the word affär never occurs and no shop stock is mentioned at all; it is also mildly counter-indicated by “nya upplagor … så länge ett motiv gick att sälja”, which describes stock being replenished rather than ageing on a shelf. Same fair species as A: plausible in the world, unanchored in the text.
